transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. An induction hob tripping your house electrics is usually an earth-leakage fault inside the hob itself—most commonly the power module or the induction coil for a specific zone leaking current to the metal chassis. It can also be that the hob is drawing too much current for the circuit, though this is less common with modern split circuits. Because this involves mains electricity and potential earth faults, please do not attempt to open the hob or test internal components yourself. However, I need a bit more detail to narrow it down safely: 1. Does the trip happen immediately when you switch a zone on, or only after some time?
2. Is it always the same cooking zone that causes it, or does it vary?
3. Have there been any spills or heavy cleaning recently that might have let moisture under the glass?

It seems to be when I've got two rings on high, and sometimes when something boils over. I don't know if it's always the same ring. There have been a couple of boil-overs, yes. Once there was a faint electrical smell after it tripped too.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Given the faint electrical smell and the fact that it trips when under load (two rings on high) or after spills, this is an earth-leakage fault. In induction hobs, this usually means moisture has tracked under the glass or a component inside (like the power module or coil for a specific zone) has failed and is leaking current to the chassis. You must not use the hob again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has inspected it. Do not try to open the hob or test internal components yourself; induction power electronics hold dangerous charges even when unplugged, and insulation testing requires specialist equipment. The engineer will likely need to check for moisture ingress first (which might just require drying out if caught early) or check a faulty power module/coil assembly. Please arrange for a professional inspection.

candidates: Earth leakage fault (induction coil or power module) (high)
Overloaded circuit / MCB tripping due to high current draw (medium)
Moisture ingress under the hob causing tracking (low)
